passages.t: The watchtower, and the righteous who live by faith
passages.happening:
‘I will stand at my guard post and station myself on the ramparts’ (verse 1), Habakkuk says, to see what God will say to him. ‘Then the LORD answered me’ (verse 2): write the vision plainly on tablets, so that a messenger may run with it. ‘For the vision awaits an appointed time; it testifies of the end and does not lie. Though it lingers, wait for it, since it will surely come and will not delay’ (verse 3).

‘Look at the proud one; his soul is not upright’, ‘but the righteous will live by faith’ (verse 4). Wealth betrays the arrogant man. His appetite is as wide as the grave, and like death he is never satisfied, gathering all the nations to himself (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
City walls had watchtowers where sentries looked out for messengers or armies, and Habakkuk pictures himself as such a watchman, waiting for God's word. Public announcements were written on tablets of clay, stone or wood so that they could be read and carried. So that a herald may run with it probably means the message should be plain enough for a messenger to read and deliver, or for anyone to read at a glance.

Verse 4 sets the proud one and the righteous one side by side in two short lines. The word for faith, emunah, usually means faithfulness: steady trust shown in a life. The proud conqueror lives by his own strength and appetite. The righteous person lives by relying on God's word, and so stays loyal through the disaster that is coming.

There is a question of whose faithfulness is meant. The Hebrew speaks of the righteous one's own faithfulness. The ancient Greek translation speaks of God's.
passages.later: Paul quotes verse 4: ‘The righteous will live by faith’ (Romans 1:17), and again in Galatians 3:11. Hebrews quotes it in the Greek form: ‘But My righteous one will live by faith’ (Hebrews 10:38).
passages.hard:
Did Paul use Habakkuk 2:4 fairly, when the prophet seems to speak of faithfulness rather than faith in Christ?

This is a real question in scholarship. The Hebrew word emunah usually means faithfulness, and in its setting Habakkuk contrasts the proud conqueror with the loyal Judean who trusts God through judgment. Some scholars argue that Paul shifted the meaning toward belief in the gospel. Others answer that in Hebrew thought trust and faithfulness cannot be separated: the faithful person is the one who trusts God's promise and so stays loyal. On this view Paul draws out what was already there, since Habakkuk's righteous one lives not by his own strength, like the proud Babylonian, but by reliance on God's word.

A further debate concerns whose faithfulness is meant. The Hebrew points to the righteous one's faithfulness, the Greek translation to God's, and some scholars read Paul's phrase from faith to faith as including God's or Christ's faithfulness as well as human trust. These notes leave the debate open. Christians agree that the verse speaks of a life that rests on God rather than on itself.
passages.asks: God told Habakkuk to wait for a vision that lingers. Ask what you are waiting on God for, and how you are living while you wait. And ask whether you live by your own strength, like the proud one, or by trust in God.

passages.t: Woe to the plunderer and the builder by bloodshed
passages.happening:
The nations will take up a taunt against the conqueror. Woe to him who piles up what is not his and grows rich on loans (verse 6). His creditors will suddenly rise against him (verse 7). ‘Because you have plundered many nations, the remnant of the people will plunder you’ (verse 8).

“Woe to him who builds his house by unjust gain, to place his nest on high and escape the hand of disaster!” (verse 9). ‘For the stones will cry out from the wall, and the rafters will echo it from the woodwork’ (verse 11).

“Woe to him who builds a city with bloodshed and establishes a town by iniquity!” (verse 12). The nations exhaust themselves for nothing (verse 13). ‘For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
After destroying Nineveh and defeating Egypt, Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar extended its control over Syria, Phoenicia and Judah, deporting peoples and collecting tribute. Nebuchadnezzar rebuilt Babylon on a grand scale, with huge walls, palaces and temples, largely paid for by the wealth of conquered peoples. The woes fit that empire closely.

The woes take the form of a taunt song, a mocking saying the nations take up against their oppressor. Each opens with woe to him who, names a crime, and announces a fitting result: the plunderer is plundered, the house built by unjust gain is shamed. The stones of the wall cry out as witnesses against the one who built it.

Verse 14 stands outside the pattern. Against the conqueror's self-made glory, the whole earth will be filled with the knowledge of the LORD's glory.
passages.later: Isaiah has nearly the same promise: ‘for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water’ (Isaiah 11:9). Jeremiah also condemned the one who ‘builds his palace by unrighteousness’ (Jeremiah 22:13).
passages.asks: The stones of a house built by injustice cry out against its builder. Ask whether anything you have built rests on someone else's loss. And ask what it would mean to build for God's glory rather than your own.

passages.t: Woe to the shamer and the idol maker, and silence before the LORD
passages.happening:
Woe to the one who makes his neighbors drink until they are drunk, in order to look on their nakedness (verse 15). He will be filled with shame instead of glory; the cup in the LORD's right hand will come round to him (verse 16). His violence against Lebanon and its animals will overwhelm him (verse 17).

What use is an idol a craftsman carves? Its maker trusts his own creation, idols that cannot speak (verse 18). Woe to the one who tells wood to wake up and silent stone to rise; it is overlaid with gold and silver, ‘yet there is no breath in it at all’ (verse 19).

‘But the LORD is in His holy temple; let all the earth be silent before Him’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The fourth woe pictures the conqueror humiliating his neighbors, and the cup of God's judgment coming back to him. Violence against Lebanon recalls the cutting of Lebanon's cedars for imperial building, something Mesopotamian kings boasted of, and the destruction of its animals.

The fifth woe mocks idols: wood and stone covered in gold and silver, with no breath in them. The conqueror's gods cannot speak.

The chapter ends in contrast. The idol is silent because it is nothing. The whole earth falls silent because the LORD is in his holy temple. Against the conqueror's self-made glory and his dumb idols stands the living God.
passages.later: A psalm mocks idols in the same way: ‘They have mouths, but cannot speak’ (Psalm 115:5). Zephaniah echoes the call to silence: ‘Be silent in the presence of the Lord GOD’ (Zephaniah 1:7).
passages.asks: The chapter ends with silence before God. Ask when you last stopped talking and simply stood before him. And ask what silent idol you have been asking to rise up and help you.
